hints: Look at what is made from what, bromoethane to ethene means an alkane derivative is becoming an alkene.
Removing HBr from a haloalkane to form a C=C double bond is elimination, not substitution.
Recall the classic condition rule, ethanolic NaOH favours elimination while aqueous NaOH favours substitution to an alcohol.
walkthrough:
**Compare reactant and product**

Think like a detective. We start with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ and end with $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$. A small molecule of $\text{HBr}$ has been lost and a double bond has formed.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 + \text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Name the reaction type**

When H and Br are removed from adjacent carbons to make C=C, that is elimination (dehydrohalogenation). Substitution would keep it single bonded and just swap Br for OH to make ethanol.

$$\text{elimination: haloalkane} \rightarrow \text{alkene}$$

**Choose the correct solvent condition**

Here is the golden rule to memorise. Ethanolic (alcoholic) NaOH, heated, acts as a base and causes elimination. Aqueous NaOH, heated, acts as a nucleophile and causes substitution.

$$\text{ethanolic NaOH} \rightarrow \text{elimination}, \quad \text{aqueous NaOH} \rightarrow \text{substitution}$$

**Match to the row**

We need elimination plus ethanol solvent. That combination gives ethene as required.

options.A: Exactly right. Ethanol as solvent with NaOH gives ethanolic conditions which promote elimination of HBr to form ethene. Well done for remembering this key distinction.
options.B: The solvent is right but the reaction type is wrong. Substitution of bromoethane would replace Br with OH to give ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, not ethene. You may have mixed up the two pathways.
options.C: The reaction type is right but the solvent is wrong. Water means aqueous NaOH, which favours nucleophilic substitution to form an alcohol, not elimination to an alkene.
options.D: Both parts point to the other pathway. Aqueous NaOH (water solvent) causes substitution to give ethanol: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{NaBr}$. This is a common trap if the two sets of conditions are reversed.
